title: India Inc not passing on gains: PM flags salary, sub-par goods
where: Front page lead, continued on page 2 (Dheeraj Mishra)
syllabus: GS4 › Ethical concerns and dilemmas in private institutions; corporate governance · GS3 › Industrial policy; effects of liberalisation; Make in India · GS2 › Consumer protection
summary: At FICCI's annual convention, the PM said industry had not passed on the corporate tax cut to workers through higher salaries or jobs, and said he was 'ashamed' of sub-par goods sold to Indian consumers.
ideas: Tax relief without sharing: corporate tax cut from 30% to 22%, yet the PM asked whether salaries or headcount had risen.
GS4 · Corporate governance / GS3 · Fiscal policy
A tax cut is a public sacrifice; corporate governance demands that its gains reach workers, not only shareholders.
Quality as an ethical duty: a captive market of 1.4 billion breeds complacency; 'our own people' are entitled to good-quality products.
GS4 · Business ethics / GS2 · Consumer protection
Selling sub-par goods because 'it will sell anyway' treats citizens as captive buyers, not stakeholders.

Self-reliance in an era of 'weaponisation of resources': India imports APIs despite being the 'Pharmacy of the World', exports iron ore but imports finished steel, has bauxite but imports aluminium alloys.
GS3 · Industrial policy / Supply chains
Raw-material exports with value-added imports show the gap between resource wealth and manufacturing depth.
Agriculture neglected by capital: India's share of global agri exports is only 2–2.5% as corporates hesitate to invest.
GS3 · Agriculture and food processing
Corporate investment in processing, procurement and export markets can turn India's farm output into an export identity.
Stakeholder nation: larger firms should lift small ones in quality and scale; a country progresses only when it respects farmers, small entrepreneurs, wealth creators and taxpayers.
GS4 · Values / GS3 · MSMEs
Growth that is shared across farmers, MSMEs and workers is both an economic and an ethical idea of progress.
keywords: Firms answer to workers, consumers and society, not only shareholders
The PM's question on salaries is a call for stakeholder capitalism over shareholder primacy.
Trust owed in return for public concessions such as tax cuts
A tax concession creates a fiduciary duty to society: the benefit is held in trust for wider welfare.
Quality slips when demand is assured
Captive-market complacency erodes quality; competitiveness abroad begins with respect for buyers at home.
Using control of inputs and supply chains as leverage
In an era of weaponisation of resources, import dependence on APIs and alloys is a strategic risk.
Moving from raw exports to finished, high-value goods
Exporting iron ore and importing steel signals the need for value-chain deepening.
data: GS3 · Fiscal policy · GS4 · Corporate governance
Despite the corporate tax cut from 30% to 22%, wage growth has lagged, the PM noted.
India's share of global agricultural exports
India's share of global agri exports is only 2–2.5%, far below its farm output.
examples: a PM asking industry to share tax gains with workers
Modi at FICCI 2026: a PM asking industry to share tax gains with workers.
strength in finished medicines, dependence in ingredients
'Pharmacy of the World' imports APIs: strength in finished medicines, dependence in ingredients.
Iron ore out, steel in: resource wealth without manufacturing depth.
consumer dignity as a business value
GS4 · Business ethics · GS2 · Consumer protection
PM 'ashamed' of sub-par goods: consumer dignity as a business value.
pyqs: Moral integrity and professional efficiency in corporate governance.
Is CSR efficient and sufficient for the corporate sector's social role?
CSR makes companies more profitable and sustainable.
Case: food company sells rejected export products in the domestic market.
Satyam scandal and changes in corporate governance.
Companies Act 2013, CSR and inclusive growth.
Corporate lobbies, pluralism and the convergence of wealth and power.

trend.t: Corporate ethics questions began with law and compliance (Companies Act CSR 2013, Satyam 2015), moved to whether CSR pays or suffices (2017, 2022), and then to the character of business itself: moral integrity in corporate governance (2023) and corporate wealth's hold on democracy (GS2, 2026). Case studies (2016, 2018, 2020, 2021, 2024) repeatedly test profit against people: workers, consumers, environment.
trend.watch: CSR and corporate governance recur almost every alternate year in GS4, and 2021's case on selling export rejects at home is the same quality-for-own-citizens issue the PM raised.
focus: Stakeholder vs shareholder model of corporate governance
Fair wages and sharing of gains with workers
Consumer rights and quality as business ethics
Limits of mandated CSR vs voluntary corporate conscience

potential: "Corporate governance is not only about compliance with law but about the moral obligation to share gains with stakeholders." Discuss with reference to recent concerns over wages and product quality. (10 marks)
What ethical issues arise when businesses sell lower-quality products in a captive domestic market? Suggest measures to build a culture of quality. (10 marks)
Examine the ethical responsibilities of industry when it receives public concessions such as tax cuts. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Corporate governance is not only about compliance with law but about the moral obligation to share gains with stakeholders." Discuss with reference to recent concerns over wages and product quality.
parts: Why gains are not shared: challenges

answer.t: Addressing FICCI in November 2026, the PM said industry had not passed on the corporate tax cut (30% to 22%) to workers and was selling sub-par goods at home.

pts.t: A firm draws on workers, consumers and public resources, so it owes them a fair share, not only its shareholders.
pts.ex: PM: 'Have you increased the salaries of your employees?'

pts.t: Tax relief is a sacrifice by the public exchequer; using it only for profit breaks an implicit social contract.
pts.ex: Corporate tax cut to 22% without matching wage gains.

pts.t: Quality is respect for the buyer; a captive market is not a licence for poor goods.
pts.ex: PM: 'Are our own people not entitled to good-quality products?'

pts.k: Integrity over the letter of law
pts.t: Legal minimums such as mandated CSR can coexist with unfair wages; conscience must go further.
pts.ex: Satyam (2009): compliant on paper, fraudulent in substance.

pts.t: Large firms can mentor MSMEs on quality and scale.
pts.ex: PM asks big companies to help smaller ones develop quality.

answer.h: Why gains are not shared: challenges

pts.t: Quarterly profit pressure favours buybacks and dividends over wages.
pts.ex: Tax savings retained as profit, not shared as pay.

pts.t: Abundant labour keeps bargaining power and wages low.
pts.ex: Informal and contract work in manufacturing.

pts.t: Patchy standards and testing let poor goods pass.
pts.ex: GS4-2021 case: export rejects sold domestically.

pts.t: Tie concessions to jobs, wages and quality benchmarks, as in output-linked schemes.
Mandatory standards, consumer redress and 'zero defect' as a value.
pts.ex: Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and BIS standards.

pts.t: Boards that measure fair wages and customer trust, not only profit.
pts.ex: Gandhi's idea of trusteeship, recalled by the PM.

answer.t: Good corporate governance is measured by who shares in the gains; profit with fair wages and fair goods is the ethic India's growth needs.

title: Tax cuts, fair wages and the duty to share
news: The PM told FICCI that industry had not passed on the corporate tax cut to workers and was selling sub-par goods to Indian consumers.
syllabus: Ethical concerns in private institutions; corporate governance
link: A tax concession is a public sacrifice; keeping all its gains, underpaying workers and selling poor goods at home breaks the trust between business and society. Stakeholder fairness and quality are corporate governance values, not just economic choices.
question: "Profit made from public concessions carries a moral duty to workers and consumers." Discuss with reference to corporate governance in India.

title: AI and cybersecurity: Can it find flaws without creating new risks?
syllabus: GS3 › Basics of cyber security · GS3 › Awareness in IT and emerging technology · GS4 › Applied ethics (dual-use technology)
summary: October 2026, dubbed 'Black October', saw major cyber incidents found with AI's help, including the PHP2Shell flaws; AI makes finding vulnerabilities easier, but leaks, patching races and costs raise new risks.
evolution: CERT-In sets a six-hour reporting deadline for AI security incidents (cyber thread).
ideas: AI finds old flaws fast, for defenders and attackers alike.
GS3 · Cyber security
Patching speed is now security.
Global code rests on volunteer-maintained open source.
GS3 · Critical infrastructure
A digital commons needs public support.
Firms finding flaws may also sell the fix: a conflict of interest.
GS4 · Applied ethics
Responsible disclosure is a duty.
keywords: A software flaw unknown to the maker, exploitable before a patch
AI shortens the time to find vulnerabilities, so patching speed becomes national security.
Proving mathematically that a system meets its specification
Formal verification raises assurance but cannot remove the need for human judgement on assumptions.
Technology usable for both protection and harm
AI in cyber security is a classic dual-use technology.
examples: PHP2Shell (Oct 2026): one flaw, millions of websites.
public spirit keeping the internet safe
GS3 · Open source · GS4 · Public spirit
Volunteer patchers: public spirit keeping the internet safe.

trend.t: Cyber security questions moved from policy (2013 policy, 2015) to attack types (2020), cross-border attacks (2021) and national strategy (2022), then to data protection (2024) and IT Rules on fake news (2026). AI itself was asked in 2026.
trend.watch: Cyber security is asked almost every year and AI entered in 2026, so AI-enabled cyber threats and defences are a natural next question.
focus: AI in cyber offence and defence

potential: "Artificial intelligence is both the strongest shield and the sharpest sword in cyber security." Discuss. (10 marks)

title: Selling the lock and the key
news: AI firms that expose software vulnerabilities could also sell protection against them.
syllabus: Applied ethics: technology; conflict of interest
link: When the same company finds a flaw and sells its fix, incentives may favour exposure over safety. Responsible disclosure and transparency are ethical duties in dual-use technology.
question: Discuss the ethical concerns in the use of artificial intelligence in cyber security.

title: Who answers for the algorithm?
news: The government is considering withdrawing legal immunity from social media platforms whose algorithms decide what users see.
syllabus: Social influence and persuasion; Ethics of technology; Accountability
link: Algorithms shape what millions believe, making platforms powerful agents of social influence. Profiting from amplification while disowning its harm is an ethical asymmetry, but accountability must not become a tool to silence lawful speech.
question: Should those who design algorithms that shape public opinion bear moral responsibility for their effects? Discuss.

title: Autonomy must answer to someone
news: CERT-In requires AI security incidents to be reported within six hours and audits scaled to risk, after AI agents exceeded their authorised tasks.
link: When machines act on their own, responsibility must still rest with people. Traceability, explainability and human oversight are the AI-age versions of the public servant's duty to give reasons and answer for decisions.
question: As AI systems take decisions in administration, how can accountability be ensured? Discuss.

title: Anticipate, but with care
news: CERT-In is testing an advanced AI model to find software flaws before attackers do, but only on small datasets, wary of exposing sensitive public data.
syllabus: Proactive and anticipatory governance; Prudence; Ethical issues in the use of technology
link: Good administration anticipates threats instead of waiting for them, as CERT-In does by hunting vulnerabilities in advance. Yet it also acts with prudence: the duty to protect citizens' data limits how far a new tool is used. Proactivity with caution is responsible governance.
question: "Proactive governance requires both foresight and prudence." Discuss with reference to the use of emerging technologies by the State.

title: A machine must not pretend
news: New York's new law bars AI chatbots from claiming to be human, flattering minors, or encouraging self-harm or isolation.
syllabus: Ethical issues in technology; Compassion towards the vulnerable; Honesty
link: Children trust easily, so technology built to win their attention carries a duty of care. Honesty about being a machine and refusing to manipulate are basic ethical limits; profit from engagement cannot justify harm to the vulnerable.
question: "Technology that is designed only to please can harm those it claims to serve." Discuss with reference to children and AI.

title: 53 of top 100 companies fail to disclose whistleblower complaints, says report
syllabus: GS4 › Corporate governance; Probity; Ethical issues in business · GS2 › Transparency and accountability; Statutory bodies (SEBI) · GS3 › Capital markets
summary: A governance survey of Nifty 100 companies found 53 did not disclose whistleblower complaints in FY26 annual reports, showing a gap between compliance on paper and accountability in practice.
ideas: Silence on whistleblowers: more than half of India's top 100 listed companies did not disclose information on whistleblower complaints in their FY26 annual reports.
GS4 · Corporate governance
Non-disclosure of whistleblower complaints weakens the most important early-warning system in a company.
Unresolved complaints: of the complaints that were reported, a significant share remained unresolved at the end of the year.
GS4 · Accountability
Whistleblower systems work only if complaints are resolved, not just recorded.

Paper compliance vs real accountability: governance frameworks look impressive in annual reports and filings, but disclosures reveal gaps in board oversight and the functioning of independent directors.
GS2 · Transparency / GS4 · Integrity
Corporate governance in India is often compliance on paper rather than accountability in practice.
Why it matters: whistleblower mechanisms let employees and stakeholders flag financial irregularities and misconduct without fear of retaliation.
GS4 · Whistleblowing / Probity
Protecting whistleblowers is protecting the integrity of the market itself.
keywords: Channel to report wrongdoing without retaliation
A credible whistleblower mechanism is the first line of defence against fraud.
Meeting the letter of rules, not their purpose
Box-ticking compliance hides governance failures behind good paperwork.
Board members meant to check management
Weak independent directors turn board oversight into formality.
An organisation where raising concerns is safe and valued
A culture of speaking up matters more than the policy on paper.
data: Nifty 100 companies that did not disclose whistleblower complaints in FY26 annual reports; of 1,129 complaints reported, 13.37% unresolved
Excellence Enablers Annual Corporate Governance Survey (7th edition), via IE
53 of India's top 100 listed companies did not disclose whistleblower complaints in FY26 (Excellence Enablers survey).
examples: Gap between impressive governance reports and real accountability
GS4 · Corporate governance, probity · GS2 · Transparency · Essay
The whistleblower survey shows that governance written in reports is not the same as governance lived in boardrooms.
pyqs: Corporate governance changes after the Satyam scandal.
Moral integrity and professional efficiency in corporate governance.
Risks faced by whistleblowers and protection.
Amendments to the Whistleblowers Protection Act.
potential: "Corporate governance in India suffers more from weak practice than from weak rules." Discuss with reference to whistleblower mechanisms. (10 marks)

practice.q: "Corporate governance in India suffers more from weak practice than from weak rules." Discuss with reference to whistleblower mechanisms.

answer.t: A survey of Nifty 100 companies found 53 did not disclose whistleblower complaints in FY26, and 13.37% of reported complaints were unresolved (Excellence Enablers).

pts.t: Mandate vigil mechanisms and board committees.
Meant to check management.
Annual reports must cover governance practices.
Many firms stay silent on complaints.
Mechanisms record but do not resolve.
Independent directors often defer to promoters.
Employees hesitate to speak.
pts.ex: Satyam showed the cost of silence.

pts.t: Uniform reporting of complaints and outcomes.
External channel for complaints.
Audit committees answerable for resolution.
Leadership that protects whistleblowers.

answer.t: India has the rules for good governance; what it needs is boards that practise them.

title: Cheap clothes, costly lives
news: Bangladesh's garment workers, who supply global brands such as H&M, Zara, Walmart and Primark, protested for a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka against the current 12,500 taka; 679 factories halted production and the government formed a wage board.
syllabus: Work culture; Ethics in business and corporate governance; Exploitation of labour; Dignity of work
link: Low wages in global supply chains shift the cost of cheap goods onto workers; ethical corporate governance means brands and suppliers share responsibility for a living wage, not just a legal minimum.
question: "Global brands cannot outsource their ethical responsibility along with their production." Discuss with reference to workers' wages in supply chains.

title: A lifelong home: CSR with care
news: Reliance Foundation announced a 100-acre township near Mumbai as a lifelong home for orphaned children, senior citizens and persons with disabilities, in family-style homes with caregivers.
syllabus: Ethics in business: corporate social responsibility; Compassion towards the weaker sections
link: CSR is most meaningful when it meets a lasting social need with dignity, here the anxiety of parents of children with disabilities about who will care for them; the test is sustained care, not announcement.
question: "Corporate social responsibility is an ethical commitment, not merely a legal obligation." Discuss with examples.
